steps.sub: The interviewer says five words and goes quiet. No spec, no schema — just you and a whiteboard. By the end of this you'll turn a vague prompt into clean classes, lean on SOLID so a senior nods instead of flinches, and pick the one or two design patterns that actually earn their place.

steps.prompt: First move when you hear 'design a parking lot' — what do you do BEFORE writing any class?

options.t: Immediately write a ParkingLot class with 200 lines.
Ask clarifying questions: vehicle types? multiple floors? how do we charge? — then list the nouns that become your classes.
Pick a design pattern first and bend the problem to fit it.

steps.why: LLD starts with requirements, not code. Clarify the scope (motorbikes vs trucks? hourly vs flat fee? multiple entrances?), then pull the NOUNS out of the problem — ParkingLot, Level, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket. Nouns become classes; verbs become methods. Jumping to code or forcing a pattern is the junior tell.
hints: A senior never writes code on assumptions. What comes before the first class?
In the problem statement, the nouns are your candidate classes.

steps.prompt: From the parking-lot prompt, sort each word: is it a CLASS (noun) or a BEHAVIOUR (method)?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin. This is how you decompose any vague LLD prompt.
hints: If you can hold it as a 'thing' in the system, it's a class.
If it's an action the system DOES, it's a method on some class.

steps.prompt: SOLID — five rules a senior reads your design against.
steps.sub: Tap each card. You don't need to recite them; you need to FEEL when one is broken.

cards.b: One class, one reason to change. A Ticket holds ticket data; it doesn't ALSO charge the credit card. Split those.
Open to extend, closed to modify. Add a new vehicle type without editing existing parking logic — add a subclass, don't touch the old code.
A subclass must work anywhere its parent does. If Truck breaks code that expected a Vehicle, your hierarchy is lying.
Small, focused interfaces. Don't force an ElectricSpot to implement methods it doesn't use. Many thin interfaces beat one fat one.
Depend on abstractions, not concretes. PaymentProcessor depends on a PaymentMethod interface, not on 'Visa' directly — so you can swap in PayPal.

steps.prompt: AI generates: Vehicle → Car → SportsCar → RedSportsCar → RedSportsCarWith20InchRims. A senior engineer winces. Which principle is screaming?
steps.sub: This is the most common LLD smell AI produces.

options.t: Single Responsibility — the class does too much.
Open/Closed plus 'composition over inheritance' — a deep, rigid inheritance tree is fragile; model the variations as DATA/components, not subclasses.
Liskov Substitution — the red car can't replace the blue one.

steps.why: Deep inheritance is brittle: every new combination (colour × engine × rims) spawns a new class, and changing the base ripples everywhere. The senior fix is composition — a Car HAS a Colour, HAS an Engine, HAS Wheels. You compose features as fields instead of exploding the hierarchy. 'Composition over inheritance' is the single most useful LLD instinct.
hints: Count the layers. What happens when you add one more variation?
Should 'red' and '20-inch rims' be SUBCLASSES, or just fields the object HAS?

steps.prompt: The handful of design patterns that actually earn their place.
steps.sub: Tap each. AI loves pattern-soup; you bring the few that solve a real problem.

cards.b: Swap an algorithm at runtime. A FeeCalculator with an HourlyStrategy or a FlatStrategy — pick the behaviour without if/else sprawl.
Centralise object creation. A VehicleFactory turns a string ('truck') into the right object, so creation logic lives in ONE place.
Pub-sub. When a spot frees up, notify the display board and the app — without the spot knowing who's listening.
Exactly one instance. The ParkingLot manager — one source of truth. Use sparingly; it's easy to abuse.
Wrap an object to add behaviour. Add 'reserved' or 'EV charging' to a base Spot without subclassing every combination.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check.

statements.t: The more design patterns you cram into the answer, the more senior you look.
statements.why: No — pattern-soup is a junior tell. Seniors use the FEWEST patterns that solve the real problem and can justify each one. An unjustified Singleton hurts you.

statements.t: 'Composition over inheritance' means prefer HAS-A relationships over deep IS-A trees.
statements.why: Right — a Car HAS an Engine is more flexible than a deep SportsCar-extends-Car-extends-Vehicle chain. Composition keeps the design bendable.

statements.t: A class that both stores order data AND sends emails violates Single Responsibility.
statements.why: Yes — two reasons to change (data shape changes, email system changes) means two responsibilities. Split into Order and an EmailService.

statements.t: You should design the full database schema before defining any classes in an LLD round.
statements.why: No — LLD is about classes, responsibilities, and relationships. Schema is a detail that follows. Start from nouns → classes → methods → interactions.

hints: Think about what makes a senior FLINCH versus nod.
Single Responsibility = one reason to change per class.

steps.prompt: Put the LLD answer flow in the order a senior runs it.
steps.sub: Same skeleton works for parking lot, elevator, vending machine — anything.
chips: Apply a pattern only where it removes real pain
hints: You can't name classes until you know what's in scope.
Patterns and the SOLID review come AFTER you have classes with responsibilities.

steps.prompt: Mid-interview, AI gives you a clean-looking parking-lot design. What's the operator's job before you present it?
steps.sub: The agent wrote the code. You still own the answer.

options.t: Read it aloud verbatim — it's already clean.
Verify the responsibilities are split (SOLID), the inheritance isn't too deep, and every pattern it used is justified — then present it as YOUR design with reasons.
Ask AI to add three more patterns to look impressive.

steps.why: In the AI era, the agent drafts; you direct and verify. You scan for SRP violations, over-deep inheritance, and unjustified patterns — then you OWN the design by explaining the tradeoffs out loud. The interviewer is buying your judgment, not the agent's typing speed.
hints: Clean-looking ≠ defensible. What's your review checklist?
You must be able to JUSTIFY every class and pattern as if you wrote it.

steps.sub: Not graded. Tie LLD to your own job hunt.

fields.label: Name a system you actually use daily — we'll use it as your LLD practice prompt:
fields.ph: e.g. Spotify, an ATM, an elevator, a food-delivery app

fields.label: What's the one LLD smell you'll now watch for in AI's code?
fields.ph: e.g. deep inheritance, a class doing two jobs, unjustified patterns
